plain_english: We'll be happy with our wealth if we've first learned to enjoy living simply. Without thrift, no amount of money is ever enough. With it, any amount is plenty. The cure for wanting more is always available — even poverty can become richness if you add thrift to it. Let's get used to ignoring flashy displays. Judge things by how useful they are, not by how fancy they look. Let food satisfy your hunger, drink quench your thirst, and keep your desires within reasonable limits. Use your body properly. Dress and live the way our ancestors did — the good ways that worked — not copying every new trend. Learn to control yourself more. Push back against luxury. Set limits on your pride. Cool your anger. Don't look down on poverty. Practice thrift, even though many people are embarrassed to do it. Use simple, cheap solutions for what your body actually needs. Lock away all those wild hopes and dreams that have no discipline. Make it your job to get your wealth from yourself, not from luck.
original_excerpt: We shall be pleased with this measure of wealth if we have previously taken pleasure in thrift, without which no riches are sufficient, and with which none are insufficient, especially as the remedy is always at hand, and poverty itself by calling in the aid of thrift can convert itself into riches. Let us accustom ourselves to set aside mere outward show, and to measure things by their uses, not by their ornamental trappings: let our hunger be tamed by food, our thirst quenched by drinking, our lust confined within needful bounds; let us learn to use our limbs, and to arrange our dress and way of life according to what was approved of by our ancestors, not in imitation of new-fangled models: let us learn to increase our continence, to repress luxury, to set bounds to our pride, to assuage our anger, to look upon poverty without prejudice, to practise thrift, albeit many are ashamed to do so, to apply cheap remedies to the wants of nature, to keep all undisciplined hopes and aspirations as it were under lock and key, and to make it our business to get our riches from ourselves and not from Fortune.

plain_english: We can never completely defend ourselves against all the bad luck that threatens us. If we spread our lives too wide, we'll feel the weight of every storm that hits. We need to keep our affairs simple and small. That way, Fortune's arrows can't find their mark. Sometimes small setbacks actually help us. And lighter troubles can cure more serious problems. When your mind won't listen to good advice and gentler methods don't work, maybe poverty, disgrace, or financial ruin is exactly what it needs. One evil cancels out another. So let's learn to eat dinner without all of Rome watching. Let's have fewer slaves to serve us. Let's buy clothes that just do their job. Let's live in smaller houses. Take the inside track — not just in races at the circus, but in the race of life. Even studying literature, which is the most respectable way for a gentleman to spend money, only makes sense if you keep it within limits.
original_excerpt: We never can so thoroughly defeat the vast diversity and malignity of misfortune with which we are threatened as not to feel the weight of many gusts if we offer a large spread of canvas to the wind: we must draw our affairs into a small compass, to make the darts of Fortune of no avail. For this reason, sometimes slight mishaps have turned into remedies, and more serious disorders have been healed by slighter ones. When the mind pays no attention to good advice, and cannot be brought to its senses by milder measures, why should we not think that its interests are being served by poverty, disgrace, or financial ruin being applied to it? one evil is balanced by another. Let us then teach ourselves to be able to dine without all Rome to look on, to be the slaves of fewer slaves, to get clothes which fulfil their original purpose, and to live in a smaller house. The inner curve is the one to take, not only in running races and in the contests of the circus, but also in the race of life; even literary pursuits, the most becoming thing for a gentleman to spend money upon, are only justifiable as long as they are kept within bounds.

plain_english: What's the point of owning thousands of books and libraries when you can barely read all the titles in your lifetime? A student gets overwhelmed by so many books, not educated. It's much better to focus on a few good writers than to skim through many. Forty thousand books burned at Alexandria. Some people praised that library as a noble monument to royal wealth, like Titus Livius, who called it "a splendid result of the taste and careful attention of the kings." But it had nothing to do with taste or care. It was just learned luxury — not even learned, really, since they collected books not to learn from them, but to show off. Just like many people today who know less about literature than we'd expect from a slave, and who use their books not for study but to decorate their dining rooms.
original_excerpt: What is the use of possessing numberless books and libraries, whose titles their owner can hardly read through in a lifetime? A student is overwhelmed by such a mass, not instructed, and it is much better to devote yourself to a few writers than to skim through many. Forty thousand books were burned at Alexandria: some would have praised this library as a most noble memorial of royal wealth, like Titus Livius, who says that it was "a splendid result of the taste and attentive care of the kings." It had nothing to do with taste or care, but was a piece of learned luxury, nay, not even learned, since they amassed it, not for the sake of learning, but to make a show, like many men who know less about letters than a slave is expected to know, and who uses his books not to help him in his studies but to ornament his dining-room.

plain_english: Get as many books as you want, but don't buy them just to show off. "It's more respectable," you say, "to spend money on books than on fancy bronze vases and paintings." No, it's not. Anything taken to extremes is wrong. What excuse is there for someone who rushes to buy bookcases made of ivory and expensive wood, collects works by unknown or terrible authors, and then sits yawning among thousands of books? He likes their spines and titles more than what's actually inside them. In the homes of the laziest people, you'll see the complete works of every speaker and historian stacked on shelves reaching to the ceiling. These days a library has become as essential to a house as hot and cold running water. I'd forgive them if they were truly passionate about literature. But they're not. These expensive works of genius, with all their beautiful illustrations, are just bought for display — fancy wallpaper with words.
original_excerpt: Let a man, then, obtain as many books as he wants, but none for show. "It is more respectable," say you, "to spend one's money on such books than on vases of Corinthian brass and paintings." Not so: everything that is carried to excess is wrong. What excuses can you find for a man who is eager to buy bookcases of ivory and citrus wood, to collect the works of unknown or discredited authors, and who sits yawning amid so many thousands of books, whose backs and titles please him more than any other part of them? Thus in the houses of the laziest of men you will see the works of all the orators and historians stacked upon book-shelves reaching right up to the ceiling. At the present day a library has become as necessary an appendage to a house as a hot and cold bath. I would excuse them straightway if they really were carried away by an excessive zeal for literature; but as it is, these costly works of sacred genius, with all the illustrations that adorn them, are merely bought for display and to serve as wall-furniture.
